finding.claim: GET /users returns the id and name of every user in whichever org the caller names. The org comes from a client-supplied query parameter. It is not tied to the caller's own org or session, and the file has no authentication or authorization check. Any caller can enumerate any tenant's users by changing `org`. This is a candidate. Auth middleware may exist outside this file, but none is visible here, and `req.pg` is attached by middleware that isn't in the file. Even with authentication in place, the org is never checked against the caller's membership.
finding.sink: req.pg.query SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE org = $1, with the rows returned via res.json

trace.note: route handler registered with no auth or authorization middleware
req.query.org is used directly as the tenant filter, with no comparison to the caller's identity or org
all matching rows are returned to the caller

finding.guards_checked: The query is parameterized ($1), so there is no SQL injection. I found no session, user or org scoping in the file, and no auth middleware is registered on app. I did not see where req.pg is set, so external middleware may enforce authentication. Even then, the org value is never compared to the caller's own org. The `/file` route is safe: the startsWith(ROOT + path.sep) check against the resolved path stops traversal. The `/count` route is safe: execFile uses constant arguments and no shell.

verdict.guard_found: none (the query is parameterized, which stops SQL injection but not the missing org authorization)
verdict.reason: db.js:8-10 matches the trace: the handler passes the client-supplied req.query.org straight to the query at db.js:9 and returns the rows, with no auth or org check, and db.js is the only file, so `app` is not exported and no other middleware can guard it. As written, req.pg is never set (nothing in this file assigns it), so the handler would throw; this finding assumes it is injected somewhere outside the repo.
